analysis.one_liner: Taxes opioid drugmakers to fund state addiction prevention and treatment grants.
analysis.headline: The opioid-manufacturer tax bill never got a committee hearing or a vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have put a new federal tax on opioid painkillers manufactured in the United States and sent every dollar collected to the Department of Health and Human Services. HHS would then hand grants to states for opioid research, abuse prevention, and treatment programs, including treatment for heroin addiction. The money would not have needed an annual vote of Congress — it would flow automatically. The bill was introduced in July 2017 and referred to three House committees: Ways and Means (which handles taxes), Energy and Commerce, and Budget. None of them ever acted on it. It received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.who_benefits: People struggling with opioid and heroin addiction and their families, through new federal grants to states for prevention, treatment, and research. State and local treatment programs would have gained a dedicated funding stream that did not depend on yearly congressional appropriations, and the excise tax would have been paid by the pharmaceutical companies that manufacture opioid drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with opioid addiction; state treatment programs

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have imposed a federal excise tax on opioid drugs manufactured in the United States, paid by the manufacturers.
Treasury would have had to transfer revenue equal to the tax collections to the Department of Health and Human Services to fund the bill's programs.
HHS would have been required to give states grants for opioid research (including heroin) and for opioid abuse prevention and treatment programs.

The funding would have been available without further appropriation and designated as an emergency requirement under the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010, so the money would not depend on Congress passing a new spending bill each year.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies that manufacture opioid drugs in the United States would pay the new excise tax. Like any excise tax, part of it could be passed on in the price of the drugs to pharmacies, insurers, and patients.

drawbacks.text: An excise tax on opioid manufacturers may be passed through to drug prices, which could raise costs for patients who legitimately use prescription opioids for pain.

The bill bypassed the normal annual appropriations process — the funding was made available without further appropriation and labeled an emergency under PAYGO — which reduces Congress's control over how the money is spent year to year.

A tax on a medical product does nothing by itself to restrict how opioids are marketed or prescribed; it raises revenue for treatment but leaves the underlying supply and prescribing practices to existing law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main purpose was to create a dedicated, automatic funding stream for state opioid prevention and treatment, paid for by a tax on the companies making the opioids. The cost falls on opioid manufacturers and, to the extent they pass the tax on, on patients and insurers buying pain medication. The design — a self-funding tax that skips annual appropriations — made the treatment money reliable, but the bill was a narrow proposal with modest stated scope, and it was never debated or amended in public, so its real-world effect was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and none of them ever reported it out; it died there when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D-NM) introduced the Heroin and Opioid Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act of 2017 on July 14, 2017.

The bill would have imposed an excise tax on opioids manufactured in the United States and transferred the revenue to HHS for state grants for opioid research, prevention, and treatment, with the money available without further appropriation under an emergency PAYGO designation.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Budget committees on the day of introduction; no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote ever followed.
The bill attracted only 7 cosponsors and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers, who never had to pay the excise tax, and no state ever received the bill's dedicated treatment grants.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opioid manufacturers, who avoided the tax

for.name: Rep. Michelle Lujan Grisham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought referrals to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Budget committees.

for.name: 7 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, the only other members of Congress listed in support of the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership (Chair Kevin Brady)
against.role: Chair of the committee with jurisdiction over the tax provision
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill after it was referred on July 14, 2017.

against.name: House Speaker
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three committees simultaneously (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Budget), splitting its jurisdiction, and no further step ever followed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record; its only listed supporters were a Democratic sponsor and 7 cosponsors, and the committees controlled by the Republican majority took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would have taxed opioids at the point of manufacture, taking money directly from companies that sell the drugs fueling the crisis to fund treatment. The bill's death left that tax unimposed.
State grants for opioid abuse prevention and treatment would have funded treatment programs and research, creating demand for treatment services.
